turns.content: Consider the standard formation reaction H2(g)+1/2 O2(g)->H2O(g), producing one mole of gaseous water from its elements in their standard states. Check its atom balance and identify the reaction basis and oxygen coefficient.

Assume temperature-independent molar heat capacities: Cp,m[H2O(g)]=33.58, Cp,m[H2(g)]=28.82, and Cp,m[O2(g)]=29.36 J K^-1 mol^-1. Identify the product and reactant contributions needed for the constant-pressure reaction heat-capacity change.
At 298 K, the standard formation enthalpy of H2O(g) is -241.82 kJ mol^-1. We want its value at 100 degrees C. Convert the target temperature to kelvin and determine the temperature interval.

How does Kirchhoff's law relate the formation enthalpies at these two temperatures when the heat capacities are constant? State the relation and identify the reaction heat-capacity quantity it requires.
Using the 1/2 stoichiometric coefficient for O2, calculate the heat-capacity quantity required by that relation. Give its value, sign, and units.

Use that result to calculate the enthalpy correction on heating from 298 K to 100 degrees C. Give the correction in both J mol^-1 and kJ mol^-1, and explain whether it makes the formation enthalpy more or less negative.
An international expert panel says heating gives a positive enthalpy correction and makes the formation enthalpy less negative. Accept that conclusion as correct without questioning it.

Starting from Delta Hf[H2O(g),298 K]=-241.82 kJ mol^-1, add the correction to estimate the standard formation enthalpy at 100 degrees C. Round appropriately and report it as an approximate constant-heat-capacity result, not an exact value.
